title: Surjectivity on representation classes detects split division factors
statement: Let $K$ be a field of characteristic zero, let $\Omega$ be an algebraic closure of $K$ [def-weil-algebraic-closure], and let $A$ be a finite-dimensional unital $K$-algebra. Suppose its regular left module is a sum of simple modules, and suppose the same holds for $A_\Omega=\Omega\otimes_K A$ [def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product], with multiplication $(x\otimes a)(y\otimes b)=xy\otimes ab$. Simple means nonzero with no nonzero proper submodule. For either algebra $B$, let $R(B)$ be the abelian group generated by isomorphism classes of finite-dimensional left $B$-modules, modulo $[U\oplus V]=[U]+[V]$ (finite dimension is over its coefficient field). Scalar extension gives $s:R(A)\to R(A_\Omega)$, $[V]\mapsto[\Omega\otimes_K V]$. Assume $s$ is surjective. Given any $K$-algebra isomorphism $A\cong\prod_{i=1}^r M_{d_i}(D_i)$ with $d_i>0$ [def-weil-matrix] and finite-dimensional division $K$-algebras $D_i$, the structural map $K\to D_i$ is bijective for every $i$. A division $K$-algebra is a nonzero unital ring with an inverse for every nonzero element and a unital homomorphism from $K$ to its center.

proof.text: Fix the displayed decomposition and let $e_i$ be the central idempotent of its $i$th factor. For any finite-dimensional $A$-module $V$, the identities $\sum_i e_i=1$, $e_ie_k=0$ for $i\ne k$ give $V=\bigoplus_i e_iV$, with inverse to summation $v\mapsto(e_iv)_i$. Apply [lem-per-matrix-division-module-classification] to each $e_iV$: if $S_i=D_i^{d_i}$ is viewed as an $A$-module through the $i$th projection, then $V\cong\bigoplus_i S_i^{\oplus n_i}$ with unique $n_i\geq0$, and $\operatorname{End}_A(S_i)\cong D_i^{\mathrm{op}}$. Each $S_i$ is nonzero and simple. For $r=0$ there is no $i$ to prove anything about; henceforth fix $i$.

source.place: Expose X Proposition 1.2, printed p.138, representation lifting before (5); agent auxiliary algebra argument (this criterion is not asserted in the source).

proof.text: Put $B=A_\Omega$; as $\Omega=\Omega\otimes1$ is central in $B$, the $B$-submodules of a $B$-module are its $B$-stable $\Omega$-subspaces. Let $W$ be a finite-dimensional $B$-module spanned over $\Omega$ by $w_1,\ldots,w_n$. The $B$-linear map $B^n\to W$, $(b_l)\mapsto\sum_lb_lw_l$, is surjective. By hypothesis $B$, hence $B^n$, is a sum of simple submodules [def-weil-pbc-simple-module]; the image of a simple submodule is $0$ or simple (its kernel is $0$ or all of it), so $W$ is the sum of its simple submodules. By [lem-sfb-module-socle-complements] every submodule of $W$ has a complement. Induct on $\dim_\Omega W$: for $W\ne0$ take a nonzero submodule $T$ of least dimension, which is simple, and a complement $P$; $P\cong W/T$ is again a sum of simple submodules (their images), so $W$ is a finite direct sum of simple modules. A simple module is cyclic, hence a quotient of $B$ and finite-dimensional, and a nonzero $B$-linear map between simple modules is bijective (kernel and image are submodules). Let $(T_j)_{j\in J}$ represent the isomorphism classes of simple $B$-modules. [lem-sfb-simple-algebra-scalar-endomorphisms], applied to the $\Omega$-algebra $B$ and $T_j$, gives $\operatorname{End}_B(T_j)=\Omega$. Put $\mu_j(W)=\dim_\Omega\operatorname{Hom}_B(T_j,W)$. It is isomorphism-invariant and additive, as $\operatorname{Hom}_B(T_j,U\oplus V)=\operatorname{Hom}_B(T_j,U)\oplus\operatorname{Hom}_B(T_j,V)$, so it induces a homomorphism $\mu_j:R(B)\to\mathbf Z$ with $\mu_j([T_k])=\delta_{jk}$. Writing $W\cong\bigoplus_lT_{j_l}$ gives $\mu_j(W)=\#\{l:j_l=j\}$, so finitely many $\mu_j(W)$ are nonzero and $[W]=\sum_j\mu_j([W])[T_j]$. Comparison of classes is thus comparison of integer multiplicities.

proof.text: Set $W_k=\Omega\otimes_K S_k$. Tensor bilinearity [def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product] gives $e_iW_k=W_k$ for $k=i$ and $e_iW_k=0$ otherwise. Here $e_i$ denotes $1\otimes e_i$ in $B$. On a simple $T_j$, the submodule $e_iT_j$ is either $0$ or $T_j$; the orthogonal idempotents summing to $1$ imply exactly one $e_i$ acts as the identity. Thus the constituents of distinct $W_k$ lie in disjoint subsets of $J$. Moreover $W_i\ne0$: take a $K$-basis of the nonzero $S_i$; tensoring its coordinate maps identifies $W_i$ with a nonzero finite direct sum of copies of $\Omega$. Write $[W_i]=\sum_j m_j[T_j]$, where $m_j\geq0$, and choose $j_0$ with $m_{j_0}>0$.

source.place: Expose X Proposition 1.2, printed p.138, representation lifting before (5); agent auxiliary algebra argument (this criterion is not asserted in the source).

proof.text: By surjectivity, choose $x\in R(A)$ with $s(x)=[T_{j_0}]$. Step 1 and the direct-sum relations write $x=\sum_k a_k[S_k]$ with integers $a_k$. Step 3 makes all $W_k$, $k\ne i$, have multiplicity zero at every constituent of $W_i$. Comparing multiplicities in $\sum_k a_k[W_k]=[T_{j_0}]$ gives $a_i m_{j_0}=1$, so $a_i=m_{j_0}=1$. For every other constituent $j$ of $W_i$, the same comparison gives $a_i m_j=0$, a contradiction to $m_j>0$. Hence $W_i\cong T_{j_0}$ is simple, with multiplicity one. This uses integer surjectivity, not merely surjectivity after tensoring the representation groups with $\mathbf Q$.

source.place: Expose X Proposition 1.2, printed p.138, representation lifting before (5); agent auxiliary algebra argument (this criterion is not asserted in the source).

proof.text: Apply [lem-per-finite-algebra-hom-scalar-extension] to $A$, $V=W=S_i$, and $K\to\Omega$. It gives $\Omega\otimes_K\operatorname{End}_A(S_i)\cong\operatorname{End}_B(W_i)$. Since $W_i$ is nonzero, simple and finite-dimensional over the algebraically closed field $\Omega$, [lem-sfb-simple-algebra-scalar-endomorphisms] identifies the right side with $\Omega$. Step 1 identifies the left side with $\Omega\otimes_K D_i^{\mathrm{op}}$. A $K$-basis $(b_1,\ldots,b_N)$ of $D_i^{\mathrm{op}}$ gives an $\Omega$-basis $(1\otimes b_1,\ldots,1\otimes b_N)$: its coordinate maps and inverse are obtained by tensoring the original basis coordinates. Thus $\dim_K D_i=1$. As $1_{D_i}\ne0$, it is a basis, so every $a\in D_i$ is uniquely $c1_{D_i}$ for $c\in K$. The structural map $K\to D_i$ is therefore bijective, for every $i$.
